description_full: Mercury General Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, engages in writing personal automobile insurance in the United States. It also writes homeowners, commercial automobile, commercial property, mechanical protection, and umbrella insurance products. The company's automobile insurance products include collision, property damage, bodily injury, comprehensive, personal injury protection, underinsured and uninsured motorist, and other hazards; and homeowners insurance products comprise dwelling, liability, personal property, and other coverages. It sells its policies through a network of independent agents and insurance agencies, as well as directly through internet sales portals in Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oklahoma, Texas, and Virginia. Mercury General Corporation was incorporated in 1961 and is headquartered in Los Angeles, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $1.4M ranks in the top quartile among Financial Services peers, improving at 5%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $235K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Mercury General Corporation is a mid-cap financial services business with a $4.6B market cap on $6.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +18% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 52% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 12% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 18pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.45x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-3.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 27% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 21% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.77, it is more defensive than the market.
About $28.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 48% in the 2022 bear market and 63% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 55% below its DCF fair value of $184, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $136 to $256 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Financial Services peers: P/E 7.1 vs 12.2, EV/EBITDA 4.1 vs 10.9 and P/FCF 4.4 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 13% below its 10-year median.
The Street target $120 on average, 45% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 13.4% annual cash-flow growth, 13pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.1%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.28).
It converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 22% return on equity.
Operating margin is running 7pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 18.0% over 3 years, 9.6% over 5 years and 7.1% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (1.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 27, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 51.4% on average.
own: Insiders own 52.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 49%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.5% (1.5% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 36 consecutive years, though it has been cut 12.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,380 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 2.7x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 5.3% a year.
That works out to $235K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.9M (3x revenue per employee).
